title: IELTS Academic Reading Practice Test 59
instructions: You should spend about 20 minutes on each passage. Answer all questions.

passages.title: Writing at the Speed of Speech
passages.text:
A. Ordinary writing is far too slow to keep up with talking, and for most of history this meant that speech was preserved only when someone reconstructed it afterwards from memory and notes. Systems designed to close that gap have been invented repeatedly and independently, wherever there was an institution that needed a verbatim record — courts, parliaments, religious instruction — and they disappeared and were reinvented several times before becoming continuous.

B. The gain comes from abandoning the alphabet rather than from writing the same letters faster. A stroke stands for a sound rather than a letter, common words are reduced to single marks, vowels are omitted or indicated by position, and the resulting shapes are chosen to be written without lifting the pen. What is produced is a different writing system that happens to record the same language.

C. That design has a consequence its users accept and outsiders find surprising. Because so much is omitted, the notes are ambiguous without context, and a writer transcribing their own notes uses their memory of the occasion to resolve what a mark meant. Notes taken by one person are therefore difficult for another to read reliably, and shorthand is a personal record rather than a shared document.

D. The skill's spread was tied to a particular labour market and disappeared with it. When a large share of business communication was dictated by one person and typed by another, the ability was a route into office employment for very large numbers of people, and it was taught at scale as a vocational qualification. Direct composition at a keyboard removed the dictation step and with it the entire occupational category.

E. The one place it has survived is the one place the alternative is not adequate. Verbatim court transcription requires accuracy under conditions that defeat automatic systems — several people speaking at once, technical vocabulary, strong accents, poor recordings — and the machine shorthand used in that setting records syllables through simultaneous key presses rather than letters. It survives because a wrong transcript in that context has consequences no other setting imposes.

F. What automatic transcription has changed is the shape of the remaining problem rather than its existence. Recognition of clear single-speaker speech is now good enough for most purposes; recognition of overlapping speakers, deciding who said what, and knowing which parts of a recording matter are not solved, and these are exactly the parts a human writer was doing without anyone noticing they were separate tasks.

passages.title: Growing It Back
passages.text:
Most animals repair injuries and a few replace whole structures, and the difference between the two is larger than it appears. Healing seals a wound with tissue that is functional and not identical to what was lost; regeneration rebuilds the original structure, in the correct proportions, with the right tissues in the right places, and stops when the structure is complete. The second requires positional information that the first does not.

Salamanders are the standard example because they do it as adults and do it repeatedly. A removed limb is replaced with a limb of the correct length, orientation and internal arrangement, and the cells that do this appear to acquire their instructions from where they are rather than from what they were. The stump knows how much is missing, which is the property that no engineered replacement has reproduced.

The comparison with mammals is where the interest lies and where the popular account misleads. Mammals are not incapable of regeneration — the liver restores lost mass, the outer skin renews continuously, young children regrow fingertips beyond a certain point — but they do not rebuild limbs, and the difference is not a simple absence of the necessary genes. Many of the same signalling pathways are present and are used differently.

Scarring is the most likely obstacle and it is a trade rather than a defect. A rapid fibrous seal closes a wound quickly, resists infection and restores a barrier, which for a large land animal with a high infection risk is worth more than a perfect rebuild that takes months. Species that regenerate well generally scar poorly, and the association is close enough to suggest that one forecloses the other.

Experimental work has produced partial successes that clarify the size of the problem. Suppressing the scarring response, supplying particular signals at the wound, or transplanting cells has produced limited regrowth in animals that would not normally manage it, and what has not been produced is a correctly proportioned structure. Growth can be induced; the instruction to stop growing at the right size and shape is the part nobody has supplied.

The medical prospect is best stated in the narrow form. Understanding how a stump determines what is missing may inform the treatment of injuries and the growth of tissue for transplant, and this is worth pursuing on its own terms; regrowing a human limb is not a near-term possibility, and describing the research that way has made honest reporting of incremental results harder for the people doing them.

passages.title: Selling the Air
passages.text:
Radio spectrum is a resource that cannot be seen, stored or manufactured, and every wireless device depends on being allocated part of it. Two transmissions on the same frequency in the same place interfere, so use must be coordinated, and the question of who decides is one of the more consequential pieces of economic administration that almost nobody outside the field has an opinion about.

Administrative allocation was the original method and its weakness is now well documented. A regulator invited applications, compared them against stated criteria and assigned licences, which produced decisions that were slow, that favoured applicants able to argue well before officials, and that gave a valuable public asset away for a fee unrelated to its worth. The process also locked bands into uses that became obsolete while the licence continued.

Auctions were introduced to fix the pricing problem and did so, with complications. Selling licences to the highest bidder establishes a price, allocates to whoever expects to make most use of the band, and raises substantial public revenue; it also allows an incumbent to buy spectrum partly to keep a competitor from having it, and produces bids that occasionally exceed what the business can support, which has damaged the buyers rather than the public.

The design of the auction turns out to matter more than the decision to hold one. Bidders want particular combinations of bands rather than isolated licences, so an auction that sells them separately can leave a firm holding a useless fragment; formats that allow bidding on packages solve this and are harder to run and to explain. Several early auctions produced poor outcomes through design faults that are now well understood and were not obvious at the time.

The unlicensed alternative has produced more value than either method and receives less attention. Bands open to any device meeting technical rules, with no licence and no auction, are where domestic wireless networking and a great deal of short-range communication happen, and the total economic activity supported by them is comparable to that of the licensed bands. The condition is that devices must tolerate interference rather than being protected from it.

What determines the right approach is the use rather than any principle. A national mobile network needs exclusive, protected, wide-area access and is well served by a licence; a device operating over a few metres does not, and requiring one would prevent the use entirely. Systems that treat allocation as a single question to be answered one way have performed worse than those that maintain both arrangements deliberately.
